issues.issue: The representation that a Party "is duly organized and validly existing, or is a citizen and resident, as applicable, and in good standing under the laws of such Party's respective jurisdiction" cannot sensibly be applied to an individual, nor can "duly qualified to do business." What Skold actually warrants here is indeterminate.

Clause (iv), "or (iv) any other contractual or other obligations of the respective Party," has no verb and does not connect to the operative "conflict with," "result in a default" or "violate" language. What is represented about other contractual obligations cannot be read from the words.

The warranty is given as to "Restoraderm Intellectual Property Rights," a term that is never defined; Section 1.20 defines "Restoraderm Intellectual Property." The scope of the litigation warranty depends on which set of rights is meant.

"Skold is not aware of any facts from which it reasonably concludes" mixes a subjective awareness test with an objective reasonableness test in one clause. Whether the warranty is breached by facts Skold knew but did not draw the conclusion from is unclear.

Skold warrants that he "holds good title" and has "full and unencumbered rights" to the Restoraderm Intellectual Property, yet Schedule 1.22 records that some of those Patent Rights had already been assigned to CollaGenex before the Effective Date. The warranty and the Schedule cannot both be literally true.

The exclusive-ownership warranty is given as to "Restoraderm Intellectual Property Rights," an undefined term differing from "Restoraderm Intellectual Property" defined in Section 1.20. Whether the warranty extends to rights (such as trademarks) outside the 1.20 definition is exactly what is left open.

Skold's performance standard is measured by "a physical person of similar financial strength, business experience and other relevant factors," a circular and unmeasurable benchmark. There is no way to determine what conduct falls below it.

A knowledge qualifier ("to the best of Skold's knowledge") is attached to a forward-looking assurance that use of the intellectual property "does not and will not infringe." Whether Skold warranted future non-infringement at all, or only present belief, is ambiguous.

The disclaimer covers "ANY PRODUCT OTHER SUBJECT MATTER OF THIS AGREEMENT," with a conjunction plainly missing, so it is unclear whether "other subject matter" is a separate disclaimed category. The reach of the disclaimer against the Section 5.2 warranties turns on that missing word.

The final sentence deems the Purchased Assets to be CollaGenex's Confidential Information, which cannot be squared with Section 8.5(a)(iii) requiring CollaGenex to transfer those same Purchased Assets to Skold on termination. Skold would hold, as owner, information he is bound to keep confidential and not use.

The obligation to seek confidential treatment is excused "save to the extent inappropriate in the case of patent applications or otherwise," and "or otherwise" swallows the qualification entirely. There is no ascertainable limit on when the duty falls away.

Section 6.3 lets a Receiving Party keep "one copy for its legal files," while Sections 8.5(a)(i), (b)(i) and (c)(i) allow retention of a copy "for archival purposes or as otherwise required by law." The two retention rights are differently worded for the same event and cannot both be the measure.

The notice duty runs to "the disclosing Parly," in lower case, whereas "Disclosing Party" is a defined term in Section 1.6. Whether the defined party or simply the owner of the misused information must be notified is left unclear.

The prohibition is qualified "[e]xcept as set forth in press releases published by CollaGenex," which makes any CollaGenex press release its own exception and defeats the restriction. The proviso barring "the financial terms of Confidential Information of Skold" is also missing a conjunction, obscuring what may be published.

Indemnity is confined to Losses "incurred in connection with or arising out of any Third Party claim," so a breach by CollaGenex causing direct loss to Skold is outside Article 7 and, under Section 7.5, also outside the exception to the damages cap. Whether direct breach damages are recoverable at all is left to be worked out between the two provisions.

Skold's indemnity is likewise limited to Third Party Claims, leaving CollaGenex's direct losses from a Skold breach of the Section 5.2 warranties outside Article 7. The relationship between this limit and the Section 7.5 liability cap is unaddressed.

Notice must be given "reasonably promptly after becoming aware" of the claim, with no outer date, and failure is excused unless the Indemnitor was "actually prejudiced." Both measures are left to argument.

The Indemnitor has one hundred twenty days to elect to assume the defense, a period that may run past the response deadline in the underlying suit, and its control lasts only "for so long as the Indemnitor is conducting a good faith and diligent defense." Neither the election window nor the diligence standard is reconciled with the Indemnitee's need to defend meanwhile.

The Indemnitee "will agree to any settlement ... that the Indemnitor may recommend" while the proviso permits it to "refuse in good faith to agree to any such settlement" involving non-monetary relief. The mandatory agreement and the reserved right of refusal are stated in the same sentence.

CollaGenex must obtain "product liability insurance" insuring both Parties, but no coverage limit, deductible, insurer standard or form is specified. What level of insurance discharges the obligation cannot be determined from the clause.

A comma splice joins the consequential-damages bar to the aggregate cap ("...THIRD PARTY CLAIMS, IN NO EVENT WILL EITHER PARTY'S LIABILITY EXCEED THE AMOUNTS PAID UNDER THIS AGREEMENT"), so it is unclear whether the Article 7 indemnification exception also carves out the cap. The punctuation determines whether indemnity obligations are capped at amounts paid.

The Term sentence is incomplete: it breaks off at "expires (the" without naming or defining the Term. When the Agreement ends, and what the parenthetical defined term was to be, cannot be read from the provision.

"Notwithstanding any other provision herein, CollaGenex may terminate this Agreement at any time after March 31, 2007" cannot be squared with Section 8.1, under which the Agreement continues until royalty and Sublicense Income obligations expire, or with the unconditional installment obligations in Section 2.3. Whether an at-will termination extinguishes accrued and future payment duties is left open.

The remedy for an uncured material breach is termination only "on a Product-by-Product and country-by-country basis with respect to the Product and country to which the breach relates," leaving no stated remedy where the breach relates to no particular Product or country. Whether a party may terminate the whole Agreement for material breach is therefore contestable.

The last sentence provides that CollaGenex "shall be entitled to receive fifty percent (50%) of such royalty or milestone payments that are paid to Skold," without saying who must remit them or on what terms. The mechanism for CollaGenex's continuing share after termination is not stated.

The first sub-item of paragraph (a) is itself labelled "(a)" rather than "(i)," while the following items run "(ii)", "(iii)", "(iv)". The mislabelling makes cross-references to Section 8.5(a)(i) uncertain.

"All amounts due and payable hereunder" is not defined to include or exclude unpaid Purchase Price installments under Section 2.3 or unearned Milestone Payments under Section 4.1. What must be paid immediately on termination is left uncertain.

This subsection requires CollaGenex to transfer the Purchased Assets back to Skold "without any payment," which cannot be squared with Section 2.1's sale of "full, complete and irrevocable right, title and interest" free of encumbrance and paid for under Section 2.3. Whether the assignment was truly irrevocable is the conflict.

The sell-off right is conditioned "if not terminated by Skold for a material breach of CollaGenex pursuant to Section 8.3," yet paragraph (b) applies only where CollaGenex terminates voluntarily under Section 8.2. The condition can never operate within the paragraph in which it sits.

The subsection speaks of Purchased Assets "relating to such terminated Products," but paragraph (b) is triggered only by termination "in whole" under Section 8.2, so there is no antecedent set of terminated Products. Which assets must be transferred on a whole-agreement termination is left unstated.

Relieving CollaGenex of all royalty and Sublicense Income payments after it terminates for Skold's breach cannot be squared with Section 8.5(d), which preserves rights accrued before termination, or with CollaGenex's retention of the Purchased Assets under Section 2.1. Whether already-accrued royalties are extinguished is the conflict.

The sentence carries no subsection number and follows paragraph (c)(i) without designation, so it is unclear whether it belongs to paragraph (c) at all or states a free-standing rule. Its placement determines whether it applies only to termination for Skold's breach.

The survival list is prefaced by "including, without limitation," so the enumerated Sections 4.8, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.6, 8.4, 8.5 and Articles 7 and 9 sit against an open general category. Whether unlisted obligations (for example the Section 5.2 warranties or Section 6.5) survive is left to argument.

The clause declares the negotiation-and-mediation procedures "the sole and exclusive means of resolving any and all Disputes" immediately after providing that a Party may pursue "any and all legal or equitable remedies" if mediation fails. The exclusivity sentence and the remedies sentence cannot both be given full effect.

A flat prohibition on assignment is followed by provisos permitting assignment to Affiliates and to "a successor to all or substantially all of the assets or line of business to which this Agreement relates," a phrase with no defined boundary. Whether a corporate acquisition passes the Agreement without consent turns on that general language against the specific prohibition.

Section 9.3 imposes a mutual further-acts duty measured by what is "necessary or appropriate," while Section 2.4 imposes a different further-assurances duty on Skold measured by "all reasonable efforts." Which standard governs Skold's post-closing cooperation is unresolved.

Force Majeure excuses obligations and removes any right to terminate for the resulting delay, which sits against the fixed calendar deadlines in Section 3.4 and the termination right in Section 8.3. Whether a Force Majeure event postpones the December 31, 2005 and March 31, 2007 diligence dates is unaddressed.

Notice is effective only on "the actual date of receipt," yet the permitted methods include registered mail and courier with no deemed-receipt rule and no proof mechanism. When a Breach Notice under Section 8.3 starts the cure clock may therefore be disputed.

The submission to the exclusive jurisdiction of Pennsylvania courts sits against Section 9.1's statement that negotiation and mediation are "the sole and exclusive means of resolving any and all Disputes." Which provision governs access to the courts must be worked out between the two.

Severance is made to depend on the Parties substituting valid provisions "by mutual consent," with the only fallback an "essential importance" test applied to the offending provision. If consent is withheld the clause supplies no operative rule for what happens to the Agreement.

The integration clause cancels the Original Agreement recited in the recitals, yet its proviso preserves "any prior agreements or assignments between the Parties that have been filed with the United States Patent and Trademark Office." Which prior instruments survive, and whether their terms still bind, cannot be settled without reading the recitals and Schedule 1.22 with this clause.

The each-party-bears-its-own-costs rule is subject to "[u]nless otherwise provided herein," and the Agreement provides otherwise in several places (Sections 3.2(c), 4.8 and Article 7). Which costs fall under the default and which under the specific allocations is not delineated.

The no-third-party-beneficiary rule sits against Sections 7.1 and 7.2, which extend indemnity to each Party's directors, officers, employees and agents, and Section 8.4, which gives Independent Sublicensees direct rights against Skold. Whether those persons may enforce is the conflict.

The Schedule lists only three patent applications, and Sections 1.22 and 1.23 define the Restoraderm Patent Rights and Restoraderm Technology by reference to it, so whether later-filed applications or technology outside those three filings is covered depends entirely on this list. The Schedule also cross-refers to "Sections 2.5 and 5.2," a numbering that does not match the table of contents for Article 2.
